title: Nuun vs Liquid IV: Which Is Better for Hydration and Hangovers?
excerpt: Nuun vs Liquid I.V. compared on sodium, sugar, caffeine, price, and taste, plus which one actually helps more after a night of drinking and why to skip caffeinated Nuun.
metaDescription: Nuun vs Liquid IV compared: sodium, sugar, caffeine, and price, plus which works better for a hangover and why to skip caffeinated Nuun around drinking.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** Nuun and Liquid I.V. are both electrolyte drink mixes, but they're built for different amounts of thirst. Nuun Sport is a light, fizzy tablet with modest sodium, very little sugar, and about 15 calories. Liquid I.V. is a stronger powder with roughly 50 to 70 percent more sodium, more potassium, and about 11 grams of sugar, designed to work like an oral rehydration drink. For a hangover, Liquid I.V. is usually the better pick because the sugar-and-salt pairing helps your gut absorb water faster. For everyday sipping or a short workout, Nuun is lighter, cheaper per serving, and easier on your calorie budget. One rule matters more than the brand: **skip the caffeinated Nuun flavors around drinking.** Caffeine on top of alcohol, or late at night after a night out, works against what you're trying to fix.

**The quick picks:**

- **Hungover, thirsty, a bit queasy:** Liquid I.V. (original), one stick in 16 ounces of water, sipped over 20 to 30 minutes.
- **Light rehydration, all-day sipping, short workouts:** Nuun Sport, one tablet in 16 ounces.
- **Watching sugar or calories:** Nuun Sport, or Liquid I.V. Sugar-Free.
- **Before bed after drinking:** a non-caffeinated Nuun or a plain glass of water. Not a caffeinated tablet.
- **High blood pressure, kidney or heart disease:** ask your doctor before using either one regularly.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article compares general label information and research. It isn't a substitute for a doctor who knows your health history. **Talk to a doctor before using electrolyte mixes regularly if** you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, heart failure, or diabetes, you've been told to limit salt, fluids, or potassium, or you take medicines that affect sodium or potassium (some blood pressure pills and water pills, for example). Product formulas change, so check the current package for exact numbers.

## Nuun vs Liquid I.V. at a Glance

These are approximate per-serving figures for the flagship versions, based on the brands' published labels at the time of writing. Both brands sell many sub-lines, so always read the box you're holding.

| | Nuun Sport (tablet) | Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier (original stick) |
|---|---|---|
| Format | Effervescent tablet you drop in water | Powder stick you stir in |
| Sodium | ~300 mg | ~500 mg |
| Potassium | ~150 mg | ~370 mg |
| Magnesium | ~25 mg | Not a significant source |
| Calcium | A small amount | Not a significant source |
| Sugar | ~1 g | ~11 g (cane sugar and dextrose) |
| Calories | ~15 | ~45 |
| Sweetener | Mostly stevia | Sugar; the Sugar-Free line uses allulose and other sweeteners |
| Added vitamins | Few in Sport (other Nuun lines add vitamins) | Vitamin C and several B vitamins |
| Caffeine | None in plain Sport; some flavors and lines contain caffeine | None in the standard Hydration Multiplier; a separate energy line has caffeine |
| Suggested water | 16 fl oz | 16 fl oz |
| Typical price per serving | Often under $1 | Roughly $1 to $1.60 depending on pack size |

The headline difference: **Liquid I.V. is the stronger, sweeter, more "medical-style" rehydration drink. Nuun is the lighter, lower-sugar, everyday option.** Most "which is better" questions come down to how dehydrated you are and whether you want the sugar.

## Who Makes Them, and Why They Taste So Different

Both started as independent brands and are now owned by large food companies. Liquid I.V. was acquired by Unilever, and Nuun by Nestlé Health Science. That matters less than the design philosophy each one started with.

**Nuun** began as a tablet for athletes who wanted to replace salt lost in sweat without the sugar load of a classic sports drink. The fizzy tablet format came from that: it's compact, it dissolves on its own, and it makes a lightly flavored, lightly salty drink. The "Sport" line is still the core product. Over time Nuun added other lines with different jobs, including versions with added vitamins, versions with caffeine, an endurance version with more carbohydrate, and a "rest" style formula aimed at evening use.

**Liquid I.V.** took its cue from oral rehydration solutions (ORS), the simple salt-and-sugar formulas that health agencies use to treat dehydration from diarrhea. It markets the idea as "Cellular Transport Technology," which is a brand name for a well-established piece of physiology: your small intestine absorbs sodium and glucose together, and water follows them. That's why Liquid I.V. deliberately includes sugar, and why it tastes sweeter and saltier than Nuun.

So the taste difference isn't an accident. Nuun is designed to be pleasant to sip all day. Liquid I.V. is designed to move water into your body quickly when you're actually short on it.

## The Biggest Difference: How Strong the Drink Is

The fairest way to compare electrolyte drinks is by concentration, meaning how salty the finished drink is, not just what's printed on the stick. Both brands suggest about 16 ounces (roughly half a liter) of water per serving, so the comparison is straightforward.

- **Nuun Sport in 16 oz:** about 300 mg of sodium in half a liter. That works out to roughly 28 millimoles of sodium per liter (millimoles are just a way of counting how many sodium particles are in the drink).
- **Liquid I.V. in 16 oz:** about 500 mg in half a liter, or roughly 46 millimoles per liter.
- **For reference, the World Health Organization's reduced-osmolarity ORS** contains 75 millimoles of sodium per liter. That's the formula used to treat real dehydration from illness.

Neither brand reaches medical ORS strength, but Liquid I.V. gets noticeably closer. Nuun sits much nearer to a standard sports drink in saltiness, which is exactly what it's for.

### Why the sugar matters more than people think

Sugar gets a bad reputation in drink mixes, and for daily sipping that reputation is fair. But in rehydration, a modest amount of glucose does a specific job. The gut has a transporter that pulls in sodium and glucose as a pair, and water follows by osmosis. This is the reason ORS works so well, and it's widely regarded as one of the most important medical advances of the 20th century for treating diarrheal illness.

Nuun Sport has about a gram of sugar, which is too little to make much use of that pairing. Liquid I.V. has about 11 grams, which is enough to take advantage of it. In practical terms, if you're meaningfully dehydrated, Liquid I.V.'s formula is better suited to getting water absorbed. If you're only slightly behind on fluids, the difference is small, and plain water plus food does most of the work anyway.

One fair criticism: Liquid I.V.'s sugar-to-sodium ratio is higher than the WHO formula, so it isn't a perfect clone of medical ORS. It's a consumer product that borrows the principle, not a medical treatment.

## Nuun vs Liquid I.V. for a Hangover

This is the use most people care about, so it's worth being precise about what an electrolyte drink can and can't do.

### What a hangover actually is

A hangover isn't just dehydration. Researchers who study it point to several overlapping causes: poor-quality sleep, inflammation, the after-effects of acetaldehyde (the toxic compound your liver makes while breaking down alcohol), low blood sugar in some people, stomach irritation, and mild dehydration. Studies have found that how dehydrated someone is doesn't line up neatly with how bad their hangover feels. That's an important point, because it means **no electrolyte drink is a hangover cure.**

What an electrolyte drink can reasonably help with is the dehydration piece. Alcohol suppresses vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you urinate more than you drink. If you also sweated on a dance floor or vomited, you've lost sodium and potassium too. Replacing fluid and some salt can ease thirst, dry mouth, lightheadedness when you stand up, and some of the headache. For the full picture on what alcohol does to your fluid balance, see our guide to [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol).

### Why Liquid I.V. usually wins the morning after

- **More sodium and potassium per glass**, which is closer to what you actually lost.
- **The sugar helps on two fronts.** It speeds water absorption, and some people's blood sugar dips after drinking, which can add to shakiness and fatigue.
- **It's still gentle enough to sip on a queasy stomach** if you drink it slowly rather than all at once.

### When Nuun makes more sense

- **You only had a couple of drinks** and just feel a bit dry. A Nuun tablet in a big glass of water is plenty.
- **You're keeping sugar low** for diet or blood sugar reasons. Nuun Sport is about 15 calories.
- **You want something to sip through the day** rather than one strong glass. Nuun's lighter taste makes it easy to keep drinking.
- **Your stomach can't handle sweet drinks** right now. Some hungover people find Liquid I.V. too sweet and salty, and a lighter Nuun goes down easier.

### How to actually use either one

1. Start with a glass of plain water if you can keep it down.
2. Mix one serving in the full amount of water the label suggests. Making it stronger doesn't make it work better and can upset your stomach.
3. Sip it over 20 to 30 minutes instead of chugging it.
4. Eat something with carbohydrates and a little salt as soon as you can. Toast, crackers, rice, or eggs all help.
5. Stop at one or two servings. More isn't better, and the sodium adds up.

Our walkthrough on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers timing and amounts in more detail, and our deeper look at [Liquid I.V. for a hangover](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover) goes through that product specifically.

## The Caffeine Problem: Avoid Caffeinated Nuun Around Drinking

This is the part of the comparison most reviews skip. Nuun sells several flavors and lines that contain caffeine, usually somewhere in the range of a cup of tea to a small cup of coffee per tablet (check the label, because amounts vary by product). The packaging can look very similar to the caffeine-free tablets, so it's easy to grab the wrong tube.

Around drinking, caffeine causes three specific problems:

**1. Before or during drinking, caffeine masks how drunk you are.** Caffeine makes you feel more alert, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol or improve your coordination and judgment. The CDC warns that mixing alcohol with caffeine can lead people to drink more than they otherwise would and to feel less impaired than they really are. A caffeinated electrolyte tablet mixed with vodka is a small version of the same problem as an energy drink and alcohol. We cover this in detail in [caffeine and alcohol](/never-hungover/caffeine-and-alcohol).

**2. At night after drinking, caffeine wrecks the sleep you need.** Alcohol already fragments your sleep in the second half of the night. Add caffeine, which can stay active in your system for many hours, and you get even less of the deep, restorative sleep that helps you recover. A lot of the "hangover" feeling the next day is really sleep deprivation.

**3. The morning after, caffeine can make some symptoms worse.** If your heart is already racing, your stomach is sour, or you feel anxious and jittery, more caffeine adds to all three. Caffeine is also a mild diuretic in people who don't use it regularly, which isn't what you want while rehydrating.

There's one nuance worth being honest about. If you drink coffee every day, skipping caffeine entirely the morning after can give you a withdrawal headache on top of your hangover. In that case, your usual morning coffee is reasonable, but get it from your usual cup, not from an electrolyte tablet that you might sip several of without counting. Keep your rehydration drink caffeine-free so you can drink as much of it as you need. Our guide to [coffee for a hangover](/never-hungover/coffee-for-hangover) explains how to handle this.

**The simple rule:** around drinking, choose plain Nuun Sport or another caffeine-free Nuun, or choose Liquid I.V.'s standard Hydration Multiplier. Read the front and back of the tube or box for the word "caffeine" before you buy.

## Which Is Healthier?

"Healthier" depends on what you're using it for.

**For daily use when you aren't dehydrated, Nuun Sport is the lighter choice.** About 15 calories and roughly a gram of sugar per tablet is easy to fit into almost any diet. Most healthy people don't need an electrolyte drink every day at all, though. Water and normal meals supply plenty of sodium and potassium for typical activity.

**For actual rehydration, Liquid I.V. is the more effective formula.** The sugar does a job, and 45 calories is trivial when you're recovering from illness, a long hot day, or a heavy night.

A few health points apply to both:

- **Sodium adds up.** US dietary guidelines suggest keeping sodium under 2,300 mg a day for most adults, and many people already exceed that from food. Two or three Liquid I.V. sticks a day adds 1,000 to 1,500 mg. Two or three Nuun tablets adds 600 to 900 mg.
- **Potassium needs care for some people.** If you have kidney disease or take medicines that raise potassium, such as some blood pressure drugs, ask your doctor before using potassium-containing mixes regularly.
- **Sweeteners are personal.** Nuun leans on stevia. Liquid I.V.'s original line uses real sugar, and its Sugar-Free line uses allulose and other sweeteners. Some people find certain sweeteners upset their stomach, especially when they're already queasy.
- **Added vitamins are a minor perk.** The B vitamins and vitamin C in Liquid I.V. won't hurt, but there's no good evidence that they meaningfully change how you feel after drinking.

## Taste, Convenience, and Price

**Taste.** Nuun is lightly fizzy and mild, closer to flavored sparkling water. Liquid I.V. is sweeter and saltier, closer to a strong sports drink. People tend to have a clear favorite. If you hate the taste of one, you'll drink less of it, which defeats the point.

**Convenience.** Nuun tablets come in a slim tube that fits in a pocket or bag, and the tablet dissolves on its own in a few minutes. Liquid I.V. sticks are individually sealed and dissolve quickly with a stir or shake. Both are easy to travel with. Nuun's tubes can let moisture in once opened, so close the cap tightly; Liquid I.V.'s individually sealed sticks don't have that issue.

**Price.** Nuun is usually cheaper per serving, often well under a dollar a tablet in multi-tube packs. Liquid I.V. typically runs about $1 to $1.60 a stick depending on pack size and store. Both go on sale often at big-box stores and warehouse clubs, so prices shift.

**Availability.** Both are sold widely in US grocery stores, pharmacies, and big-box retailers, as well as online.

## Honest Pros and Cons

### Nuun Sport

**Pros**
- Low sugar and about 15 calories per tablet
- Lighter, fizzy taste that's easy to sip all day
- Includes small amounts of magnesium and calcium
- Usually cheaper per serving
- Compact tube is very portable

**Cons**
- Less sodium and potassium than Liquid I.V., so less suited to real dehydration
- Too little sugar to make much use of the sodium-glucose effect
- Several flavors and lines contain caffeine, and they're easy to confuse with the caffeine-free ones
- Opened tubes can pick up moisture

### Liquid I.V. Hydration Multiplier

**Pros**
- Stronger formula that borrows the proven salt-plus-sugar ORS principle
- More sodium and potassium per serving
- Well suited to hangovers, illness recovery, and hot days
- Individually sealed sticks
- Standard Hydration Multiplier is caffeine-free

**Cons**
- About 11 grams of sugar per stick (there is a sugar-free version)
- Sweeter, saltier taste that some people dislike
- More expensive per serving
- Sodium adds up fast if you use several a day
- Marketing language makes it sound more novel than it is

## How They Compare to Other Options

If neither brand quite fits, you have alternatives:

- **Pedialyte and other ORS-style drinks** are closer to medical rehydration strength and are a solid choice when you've been vomiting.
- **LMNT** is much saltier and sugar-free, aimed at heavy sweaters and low-carb eaters. Our [LMNT vs Liquid I.V. comparison](/never-hungover/lmnt-vs-liquid-iv) explains when that makes sense.
- **A homemade drink** of water, a pinch of salt, a little sugar or juice, and a squeeze of citrus costs pennies. See our [homemade electrolyte drink](/never-hungover/homemade-electrolyte-drink) recipe.
- **Plain water and a salty snack** handle mild dehydration perfectly well for most people.

For a side-by-side of the most popular options, see our [electrolyte drinks for hangover comparison](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared).

## When to See a Doctor

Electrolyte drinks are for ordinary, mild dehydration. Some situations after drinking need real medical care, and no drink mix is a substitute.

**Get medical help right away (call 911 in an emergency) if you or someone else:**

- Can't keep any fluids down for many hours, or keeps vomiting
- Is confused, very hard to wake, or passes out
- Has slow or irregular breathing, seizures, or blue-tinged or very pale skin, which can be signs of alcohol poisoning
- Has a racing or pounding heart that doesn't settle, or chest pain
- Hasn't urinated in many hours, or has very dark urine despite drinking fluids
- Vomits blood or material that looks like coffee grounds

**Also talk to a doctor if** you regularly get shaky, sweaty, or anxious the morning after drinking and those symptoms ease only when you drink again. That pattern can be a sign of alcohol withdrawal, which is worth a straightforward, confidential conversation with a doctor. And if you have heart, kidney, or blood pressure problems, ask before using high-sodium drinks.

## A Note on DHM

People shopping for electrolyte drinks are often trying to feel better after social drinking, so it's worth mentioning DHM (dihydromyricetin), a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. It works on a different part of the problem than electrolytes: researchers have studied it for its effects on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol acts in the brain. Most of that research is in animals and lab models, with limited human data, so it's promising rather than settled. There is no good evidence that DHM replaces rehydration, and it doesn't make heavy drinking safe.

If you want to try it alongside sensible drinking and a good electrolyte drink, popular choices include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [guide to preventing a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence, like pacing your drinks and eating beforehand.

## The Bottom Line

- **For a hangover or real dehydration, Liquid I.V. is usually the better choice.** More sodium, more potassium, and enough sugar to help your gut absorb water.
- **For light, everyday hydration or short workouts, Nuun Sport is lighter and cheaper**, with almost no sugar.
- **Avoid caffeinated Nuun around drinking.** Caffeine masks intoxication, disrupts the sleep you need to recover, and can worsen a racing heart or upset stomach.
- **Neither is a hangover cure.** They help with the dehydration piece. Sleep, food, time, and drinking less do the rest.
- **Watch your sodium** if you use several servings a day, and talk to a doctor first if you have blood pressure, heart, or kidney concerns.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Is Nuun or Liquid I.V. better for a hangover?**

Liquid I.V. is usually the better pick for a hangover. It has more sodium and potassium per serving and about 11 grams of sugar, which helps your gut absorb water faster. Nuun Sport is lighter, with about 300 mg of sodium and almost no sugar, so it's better for mild dehydration or all-day sipping. Neither one cures a hangover; they only help with the dehydration part.

**Does Nuun have caffeine?**

The plain Nuun Sport tablets don't, but several Nuun flavors and product lines do contain caffeine, and the packaging can look similar. Check the label for the word "caffeine" before you buy. Around drinking, choose a caffeine-free version, because caffeine can mask how drunk you feel, disrupt sleep, and worsen a racing heart or upset stomach.

**Which has more electrolytes, Nuun or Liquid I.V.?**

Liquid I.V. has more of the two electrolytes that matter most for rehydration. A standard stick has about 500 mg of sodium and 370 mg of potassium, compared with roughly 300 mg of sodium and 150 mg of potassium in a Nuun Sport tablet. Nuun adds small amounts of magnesium and calcium that Liquid I.V. doesn't emphasize. Formulas change, so check the current label.

**Is Nuun healthier than Liquid I.V.?**

For everyday sipping when you aren't dehydrated, Nuun Sport is lighter, at about 15 calories and roughly 1 gram of sugar per tablet. For actual rehydration, Liquid I.V.'s sugar has a purpose: it helps your body absorb sodium and water. Both add sodium, so if you have high blood pressure, kidney disease, or heart problems, ask your doctor before using either one regularly.

**Can I drink Nuun or Liquid I.V. while drinking alcohol?**

You can sip a caffeine-free version between alcoholic drinks to help keep up with fluids, but it won't lower your blood alcohol or prevent a hangover. Don't mix caffeinated Nuun with alcohol or use it as a mixer, since caffeine can make you feel less drunk than you are. Pacing your drinks and alternating with water matter more than which electrolyte brand you choose.

**Can I take Nuun or Liquid I.V. before bed after drinking?**

A caffeine-free option is fine before bed, along with a glass of water. Many people prefer Nuun at night because it's lighter and almost sugar-free. Avoid any caffeinated tablet, since alcohol already disrupts sleep and caffeine makes that worse. Don't overdo the amount, or you'll be up during the night to use the bathroom.

**How many Nuun tablets or Liquid I.V. sticks can I have in a day?**

Follow the label. For most healthy adults, one or two servings after a night of drinking is plenty. Each Liquid I.V. stick adds about 500 mg of sodium and each Nuun Sport tablet about 300 mg, and most adults are advised to stay under about 2,300 mg of sodium a day from all sources. If you have heart, kidney, or blood pressure concerns, ask your doctor what's right for you.
